title: Salt in Beer Beyond Gose | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewers use salt in beer beyond gose: sodium and chloride in water, salted stouts and lagers, black salt and how much to add per litre.
teaser: Gose is the famous salty beer. It is not the only one where a little salt makes the difference.
standfirst: Salt rounds out malt, fills in thin beers and can turn a stout into salted caramel. Too much and the beer tastes like the sea. Here is how to work out the right amount.
sections: What salt actually does to flavour

Table salt is sodium chloride. In beer, the two halves do slightly different jobs. Chloride makes beer taste fuller and rounder, which is why brewers add calcium chloride to soften hoppy beers and boost malty ones. Sodium, at low levels, suppresses bitterness and makes sweetness taste rounder. At higher levels it tastes salty and then harsh.

Standard brewing guidance keeps sodium below about 100 to 150 mg/L in most beers. Under roughly 50 mg/L, most drinkers will not taste salt at all. They will just notice that the beer tastes a bit fuller. That is the range where salt works beyond gose.
Do the arithmetic before you add

Sodium chloride is about 39% sodium and 61% chloride by weight. So 1 gram of salt in 20 litres adds roughly 20 mg/L of sodium and 30 mg/L of chloride. Double it and you double both.

Before adding anything, check what your water already contains. Many Indian borewell waters carry noticeable sodium, sometimes well over 50 mg/L. Softened water can carry more. A beer brewed on that water may already be at your limit. Get a water report or a basic test before you start. Our guide to brewing with packaged drinking water covers a cleaner starting point.
Use plain salt, not table salt with extras

Use salt without added iodine or anti-caking agents. Iodised table salt can leave a faint chemical note. Anti-caking agents may cloud the beer. Pure sea salt, kosher salt or a food grade brewing salt all work. Rock salt, or sendha namak, is mostly sodium chloride and works too.

Black salt, or kala namak, is a different thing. It contains sulphur compounds that give it the eggy aroma of chaat and chaas. In a sour beer that can be charming. In a lager it reads as a fault. Use it only on purpose.
Salt in stouts and dark beers

Salt and dark malt get on well. A gram or two of salt in 20 litres of sweet or milk stout lifts the chocolate and caramel notes and cuts the cloying edge, the way salt works in salted caramel. Oyster stout, an old English idea, gets part of its character from the faint salinity of oysters or their shells, which some brewers add to the boil.

For a deliberate salted caramel stout, brewers often go higher, to 3 to 5 grams in 20 litres. That puts sodium around 60 to 100 mg/L. Add it in steps after fermentation, tasting each time, rather than all at once in the boil.
Salt and hops do not always get on

Chloride rounds out a beer, while sulphate sharpens hop bitterness. Brewers talk about the sulphate to chloride ratio for this reason: a hoppy pale ale might lean towards sulphate, a malty stout towards chloride. Adding table salt pushes the balance towards chloride, along with sodium.

In a crisp, bitter IPA that can blur the hop edge and make the beer taste softer and flabbier than intended. In a hazy IPA, where brewers already favour chloride for a softer mouthfeel, a pinch can work, but there are cleaner ways to add chloride. Calcium chloride gives you the fullness without sodium. Calcium also helps the mash and the yeast too.

So reach for sodium chloride when you want the specific effect of sodium: a rounder sweetness, less perceived bitterness or an actual salty note. If you only want more body, calcium chloride is usually the better tool.
Salt in lagers and light beers

A pinch of salt can help a thin, light lager taste less watery. The idea is the same as the salt rim on a glass of Mexican-style lager with lime. In the beer itself, keep it subtle: 0.5 to 1 gram in 20 litres, adding 10 to 20 mg/L of sodium, is enough to notice body without tasting salt.

The one floor detail to respect: dissolve the salt fully in a little boiled water before it goes into the beer. Undissolved crystals sitting at the bottom of a keg can give the first few glasses a sharp, salty hit.

Gose is the classic salted wheat beer, but salt suits most tart, fruity beers. A pinch rounds the acidity in a Berliner weisse or a fruited kettle sour. Indian flavours work well here: cumin with black salt in a chaas-style sour, or salt with a fruit like guava or kokum. Our guide to brewing a gose at home shows the classic method.

Many brewers target sodium of 100 to 200 mg/L or more in these beers, where salt is meant to be noticed. Even then, sneak up on it. Saltiness grows as the beer warms in the glass.

Salt is a seasoning. Seasoning is about balance with everything else in the glass. Judging that balance in a stout, a lager and a sour is a style skill. It is easier to learn with guidance than by dumping batches.

Your first step: dissolve 1 gram of plain salt in 100 millilitres of water, then add drops to a glass of your usual beer. Note the point where the beer tastes fuller and the point where it tastes salty.
faqs: How much salt can I add to beer?
In most beers, keep sodium below about 100 to 150 mg/L. One gram of salt in 20 litres adds about 20 mg/L of sodium and 30 mg/L of chloride.
Can I use iodised table salt in beer?
It is better not to. Iodine and anti-caking agents can add off-notes or haze. Use plain sea salt, kosher salt or rock salt.
A little salt often lifts chocolate and caramel notes and cuts sweetness, much like salted caramel. Add it in small steps and taste each time.
